about.title: Los Altos Hills Slip & Fall Claims
about.longDescription: Los Altos Hills is a quiet, low-density community in Santa Clara County, built across rolling hills with winding roads like Page Mill Road and Purissima Road connecting private estates, equestrian properties, and a handful of shared community spaces. Because so much of the town is residential rather than commercial, slip-and-fall claims here often involve poorly lit walkways, sloped or gravel driveways, unmaintained stairs, or hazards on shared trails and common areas within gated communities. California law requires showing that a property owner knew, or reasonably should have known, about the dangerous condition and failed to fix it or warn visitors. That makes early documentation critical — photos of the hazard, notes on lighting or weather conditions, and any available surveillance or doorbell camera footage before it's deleted. LawProactive doesn't file claims or give legal advice; we simply connect injured residents and visitors with an independent attorney who can evaluate the specific property, the hazard, and the notice question at no upfront cost.

whyChoose.title: Why This Matters in Los Altos Hills

items.title: Notice Is Often the Hardest Part to Prove
items.desc: Because so many falls here happen on private estates or shared community land, proving the owner knew or should have known about a hazard takes careful investigation. An attorney can help gather maintenance records, prior complaints, or inspection history to build that case.

items.title: Evidence Disappears Fast
items.desc: Doorbell cameras, security footage from gated properties, and even the hazard itself (a wet step, a loose rail) can be gone within days. Acting quickly to document and preserve this evidence matters more than most people realize.

items.title: Comparative Fault Won't Automatically Bar Your Claim
items.desc: Under California's pure comparative fault rule, even if you're found partly responsible for a fall, you can still pursue compensation — it's simply reduced by your share of fault. An attorney can help make sure your side of the story is fairly represented.

items.question: I fell on a neighbor's private driveway in Los Altos Hills — can I still make a claim?
items.answer: Yes, private property owners in California owe visitors a duty to address known hazards, whether it's a residential driveway or a business. The key question is whether the owner knew, or reasonably should have known, about the condition that caused your fall. An independent attorney can look at the specific circumstances and let you know how strong the claim may be.

items.question: How long do I have to file a premises liability claim in California?
items.answer: Generally, you have two years from the date of the fall to file a lawsuit, though claims against a public entity (like a city-owned trail or facility) usually require a much shorter notice period. Because Los Altos Hills has a mix of private estates and shared or public spaces, it's worth confirming ownership of the property early. Waiting too long can mean losing the right to pursue a claim at all.

items.question: What should I do right after a fall on someone else's property?
items.answer: If you're able, take photos of the exact spot, the lighting, and any hazard like a wet surface, loose step, or debris. Ask whether there's any surveillance or camera footage nearby, since it may only be kept for a short time before being overwritten. Getting medical attention and writing down what happened while it's fresh will also help if you decide to speak with an attorney.
